name: Abbasid Caliphate
line: Seek knowledge from every quarter, test it, write it down and share your table.

quote.text: We ought not to be ashamed of appreciating the truth and of acquiring it wherever it comes from, even if it comes from races distant and nations different from us.
quote.source: On First Philosophy, 9th century, trans. Alfred L. Ivry, 1974

quotes.text: The seeker after the truth is not one who studies the writings of the ancients and, following his natural disposition, puts his trust in them, but rather the one who suspects his faith in them and questions what he gathers from them.
quotes.source: Doubts Concerning Ptolemy, 11th century, trans. A. I. Sabra

quotes.text: The finest seat in this world is the saddle of a swift horse, and the best companion for all time is a book.
What is easiest and most useful in arithmetic, such as men constantly require in cases of inheritance, legacies, partition, law-suits, and trade.
quotes.source: Preface to The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing, c. 820, trans. Frederic Rosen, 1831

quotes.text: To thirst after a comprehension of things as they really are was my habit and custom from a very early age.
quotes.source: Deliverance from Error, c. 1108, trans. W. Montgomery Watt, 1953

quotes.text: The book is a companion that does not flatter you, a friend that does not tempt you and a comrade that does not weary you.

words.usage: The caliphs’ library in Baghdad, linked with translators and astronomers. How large and how formal it was is still debated.
Learning of every kind, religious and worldly. Seeking it was held to be a duty.
Knowledge joined to judgement. Also used for philosophy and for the sciences inherited from the Greeks.
The cultivation expected of an educated person: wit, wide reading, tact and good Arabic.
The object the age fell in love with. Baghdad’s book market had about a hundred shops by 900.

words.meaning: A paper seller, copyist and bookseller
words.usage: The trade that made a city of readers. The street of the warraqs was where scholars met.
Made from rags. It reached Baghdad in the late eighth century and replaced papyrus and parchment in government offices.
For two centuries, nearly every Greek work of science and philosophy that could be found was put into Arabic.
The tradition of Aristotle and Plato carried on in Arabic by al-Kindi, al-Farabi and their successors.
The practice of arguing about God, justice and free will by reasoned debate.
A debate held before an audience under rules of courtesy, often between people of different faiths.

words.meaning: A sitting; a salon or session
words.usage: A gathering in the house of a patron or scholar for poetry, music, argument and food.
The list of people through whom a report has passed, name by name, back to its source.
Written permission from a teacher to pass on a book you have studied with them.
One of al-Khwarizmi’s two operations for solving an equation. It gave the world the word algebra.
The practical mathematics of merchants, surveyors and tax officials.
The sign for nothing in the Indian system of numerals. The words cipher and zero both come from it.
Tables for finding the positions of sun, moon and planets, checked against new observations.
A brass instrument for telling the time, finding the direction of Mecca and measuring the height of stars.
A public hospital with wards, a pharmacy and salaried physicians, where treatment was free.
The art of al-Razi and his colleagues, built on Galen and corrected by case notes.
The origin of the word chemistry, and of laboratory methods such as distilling and crystallising.
Baghdad’s markets were arranged by trade: perfumers, cloth sellers, booksellers, cooks.
A merchant could write one in Baghdad and have it honoured far away. The word cheque is often traced to it.

words.meaning: A vizier; the caliph’s chief minister
words.usage: The head of the administration. The Barmakid family held the office with famous generosity until their fall in 803.
The title of the head of the Muslim community. The Abbasids claimed it through the Prophet’s uncle al-Abbas.
The official name al-Mansur gave his new capital. Everyone went on calling it Baghdad.
The long formal poem in a single rhyme, the great form of Arabic verse.
Short comic episodes about an eloquent trickster, invented by al-Hamadhani in the tenth century.
The teller of tales in the coffee houses of later centuries, heir to the storytellers of the Abbasid street.
The chief instrument of the court. The European lute takes its name from al-ud.

words.meaning: A journey, especially one in search of knowledge
words.usage: Scholars travelled for years to hear a text from someone who had heard it from its author.

practices.name: The scholar’s hour
practices.instructions: Give the first clear half hour of the day to learning something hard: a proof, a language, a chapter of history, an instrument. Sit at a table with paper and pen. Read or work for twenty minutes, then spend five writing down in your own words what you now know and one question you still have. Keep the same subject for the whole Onda.
practices.why: The scholars of Baghdad treated study as a daily duty and a pleasure. Al-Jahiz rented booksellers’ shops overnight in order to read through their stock.
variations: Study with a partner and question each other.
Read a primary source in place of a summary.
Teach what you learned to someone before noon.

practices.name: Name your source
practices.instructions: Pick one thing you know, a fact, a recipe, a rule of thumb, and write where you learned it: a person, a book, a site. If you do not know, say so, and try to find out. Abbasid scholars cited their chain of transmitters for a saying. Naming your source makes you a more honest speaker and a better learner.
practices.why: The rule of this Onda is to name your source. In Abbasid learning, a statement was only as good as its chain of transmission, the isnad. A habit of naming where you learned something is the modern form.
variations: Name three sources for one claim.
Do it for an opinion of your own.
Thank the person who taught you.

practices.name: Copy a line into your notebook
practices.instructions: Choose one line you have read or heard this morning and copy it into a notebook, with its source and the date. The rule is to write it down today. The great Baghdad scholars filled sheets of paper, which had just come west from China. A page of good lines is a library of one.
practices.why: Paper arrived in Baghdad around 751 and made a culture of books possible. The warraqin, paper sellers and copyists, filled the booksellers’ markets. Copying a line is a little of that world.
variations: Copy a line you disagree with.
Copy a proverb in two languages.
Copy a line for someone else.

practices.name: Wash and scent your hands
practices.instructions: Wash your hands slowly, with warm water and soap, and finish with a drop of scent, such as rosewater, lavender or orange blossom. A servant brought a basin and ewer to each guest in Baghdad, and perfumes were passed. Take a minute for yourself, and dry your hands with care. It is a small luxury that starts the day pleasantly.
practices.why: Washing the hands before and after meals was a courtesy in the Abbasid house, and scent was part of a civilised life. It is an easy pleasure to borrow.
variations: Use rosewater.
Wash a guest’s hands, with a jug and basin.
Do it before and after every meal today.

practices.name: A line of calligraphy
practices.instructions: Draw one Arabic letter, such as alif, a single vertical stroke, again and again, as slowly and steadily as you can. Or write your name in any beautiful script. Baghdad’s calligraphers, such as Ibn al-Bawwab, perfected the rounded cursive hands. The point is the attention. Put your best line on the wall.
practices.why: Ibn al-Bawwab (died 1022) is said to have refined the proportioned cursive scripts. Even one slow, perfect line is an honest pleasure and a lesson in patience.
variations: Use a flat-nibbed pen or marker.
Try your name in a script you do not know.
Look up a master’s page first.

practices.name: A little algebra before breakfast
practices.instructions: Solve one small problem with unknowns before you eat: if three baskets and two apples weigh eight and one basket and two apples weigh four, how much is a basket? Al-Khwarizmi called the method al-jabr, restoring: moving a term to the other side to balance it. Work it out on paper, and enjoy the click when it comes.
practices.why: Algebra takes its name from al-jabr in al-Khwarizmi’s book of about 820. It was written to solve practical problems of inheritance, trade and land, and is still a good morning exercise.
variations: Make up a problem for someone else.
Try a puzzle with two unknowns.
Look up how al-Khwarizmi did it.

practices.name: Render it
practices.instructions: Take one paragraph each day and carry it into another form. Translate a few lines from a language you are learning. Or rewrite a technical passage so that a twelve-year-old would follow it. Or put a poem into plain prose. Compare your version with the original line by line. Note the one place where you had to choose between the letter and the sense.
practices.why: Hunayn ibn Ishaq and his school collected several manuscripts of each Greek book, compared them and translated for the sense. Translation is the closest reading there is.
variations: Translate the same passage twice, a week apart, and compare.
Translate with a friend who knows the language better.
Translate a recipe, then cook from your version.

practices.name: Doubt and test
practices.instructions: Choose one thing you believe because you were told it: a claim in the news, a rule of thumb, a fact about your own habits. Write it down. Then check it by the most direct means you have. Measure, count, time it, look it up in two independent sources, or try it. Write what you found beside the claim. One claim a day.
practices.why: Ibn al-Haytham, born in Basra, wrote that a seeker of truth must make himself the enemy of all that he reads. He tested how vision works with a dark room and a pinhole.
variations: Repeat someone else’s simple experiment at home.
Keep a page of things you were wrong about.
Ask an expert how they know.

practices.name: Learn from someone you disagree with
practices.instructions: Choose someone whose views you do not share and ask them a real question about what they think, and why. Listen to the whole answer. Find one thing you can take from it. The rule of this Onda is to take the truth from wherever it comes. Al-Kindi said we should not be ashamed to accept truth from any source, even from peoples far from us.
practices.why: Al-Kindi wrote that we ought not to be ashamed of acquiring truth from any source, even from races distant and different from us. It is a good motto for any open-minded person.
variations: Do it with someone from another field.
Do it by reading, not talking.
Thank them for the one good thing.

practices.name: A friendly disputation
practices.instructions: Pick a friend and a question, and hold a short munazara, a disputation: each in turn states a case, answers the other’s, and then both say what they have learned. Argue the point and honour the person. The aim is to find out, not to win. Shake hands at the end, and say what changed your mind.
practices.why: Formal disputation, munazara, was a major form of Abbasid intellectual life. The best of it combined a sharp argument with a graceful respect for the other side.
variations: Do it on a trivial question for fun.
Switch sides halfway.
Do it in writing.

practices.name: Lend or return a book
practices.instructions: Lend a book to someone who would enjoy it, with a note, or return one you have borrowed, with a note of thanks. Books were lent freely among scholars, and returning one late or damaged was bad form. Pick the book that is just right for the person. Then ask them next week what they thought.
practices.why: In Abbasid learning, books were lent, copied and passed on, and returning them in good order was a mark of good manners. A well-chosen loan is also a gift.
variations: Lend a book you love.
Return something that has been on your shelf too long.
Join or start a book swap.

practices.name: A shop you would not enter
practices.instructions: Visit a bookshop, a library or a secondhand market, and choose a book from a shelf you would never usually look at. Read the first page, and take it home if you like it. Al-Jahiz, who loved books, would hire a bookseller’s stall overnight to read it all. Follow your curiosity a short way.
practices.why: Al-Jahiz is said to have read all night in the booksellers’ shops of Baghdad. A visit to a shelf you do not know is a small version of his habit.
variations: Choose by the cover.
Ask the bookseller what they would read.
Read a chapter at a café.

practices.name: The majlis
practices.instructions: Hold a sitting. Invite one person or several, in your home or by call. Put out tea and something sweet. Set one question for the evening and let each person speak to it in turn before anyone answers anyone. Include a poem, a song or a story. The host’s task is to see that every guest is heard and that no one leaves hungry.
practices.why: The salons of viziers, physicians and booksellers were where Abbasid culture happened. Muslims, Christians, Jews and sceptics debated in them under rules of courtesy.
variations: Ask each guest to bring one thing to read aloud.
Agree at the start that no one may quote an authority in place of a reason.
Hold it outdoors after dark.

practices.name: Read the sky
practices.instructions: Go out after dark and look up for ten minutes. Find the moon and note its phase. Find one bright star and learn its name: Aldebaran, Altair, Vega, Deneb, Betelgeuse and Rigel all come from Arabic. Note where it stands compared with a roof or a tree, and look again at the same hour tomorrow. On cloudy nights, read a page about the stars.
practices.why: Al-Mamun’s astronomers measured the size of the Earth from the plain of Sinjar and checked Ptolemy’s tables against the sky. About two hundred stars still carry Arabic names.
variations: Follow the moon through a whole month.
Find the direction of sunrise and mark how it shifts.
Use a free star chart to learn one constellation a week.

practices.name: Leave room at the table
practices.instructions: Set one more place at the table than you need, and cook enough for it. If someone comes, welcome them, and if not, send the extra to a neighbour or save it for tomorrow. The last rule of this Onda is to leave room at the table. A good majlis host sees that no one leaves hungry. Make a habit of a little too much.
practices.why: Generosity at the table was a mark of Abbasid civilisation, and of Arab hospitality older than it. Leaving a place open is a practical way of saying that a guest is welcome.
variations: Invite someone at short notice.
Share a dish with the person next door.
Leave a seat free and see who fills it.

practices.name: Capping verses
practices.instructions: Play the game of the majlis: one person gives a line of poetry or a line of any song, and the next must answer with a line that begins with the last letter or word of that one. Play with a friend, or with a poem book open. Laugh when you stumble. It is a quick, friendly test of memory and wit.
practices.why: Riddles and capping verses were games of the Baghdad salon, and poets played them for sport. A capping game is easy to start and easy to enjoy.
variations: Play it with proverbs.
Play it by text with a faraway friend.
Play it with a child, with simple words.

practices.name: A cold sharab
practices.instructions: Stir a spoonful of fruit syrup, pomegranate, rose, lemon or quince, into a glass of cold water, and drink it slowly. The words syrup, sherbet and sorbet all come from the Arabic sharab. Make a jug for friends and enjoy the colour. It is a cool pleasure for a warm evening.
practices.why: Fruit syrups stirred into cold water were a favourite refreshment of Baghdad. The word sherbet and its cousins came west through the Arabic sharab, a drink.
variations: Make it with real pomegranate juice.
Add fresh mint leaves.
Make a jug for a gathering.

practices.name: Listen to the oud
practices.instructions: Play an oud improvisation by Munir Bashir, Naseer Shamma or another master, and do nothing else for fifteen minutes. Listen with eyes closed. The oud is the short-necked lute of the Abbasid court, said to have been refined in Baghdad by Ziryab and others. Follow how the melody wanders and returns.
practices.why: The oud was the great instrument of Abbasid music, and a concert instrument today. Listening to a taqsim, an improvisation, is a pleasure that slows the heart.
variations: Listen to Iraqi maqam instead.
Listen with a cup of tea.
Look up the story of the instrument first.

practices.name: A book market morning
practices.instructions: Spend a morning in a secondhand book market, a library or a bookshop, as on Friday along al-Mutanabbi Street in Baghdad, where booksellers still fill the street with stalls. Browse, talk to a seller, find one book that surprises you, and read the first pages over a cup of tea. Leave with one book and one conversation.
practices.why: Al-Mutanabbi Street is Baghdad’s booksellers’ street, a Friday gathering of readers and poets, named after the tenth-century poet. It continues a very old tradition of the city.
variations: Go with a friend and swap picks.
Set a small budget and keep to it.
Buy a book for someone else.

practices.name: A night of stories
practices.instructions: Gather friends or family for an evening of stories in the manner of the hakawati, the storyteller: each person tells one tale, with a beginning, a twist and a stop at the best moment. Scheherazade kept a king listening by stopping in the middle. Serve tea and sweets. Leave the last story unfinished until next week.
practices.why: The Thousand and One Nights gathers tales told by Scheherazade, each one cut off at a cliffhanger. Storytellers, hakawatis, held audiences in Baghdad’s coffeehouses for centuries.
variations: Tell a story from your own childhood.
Tell one from the Nights.
Stop mid-story and see who can’t wait.

immersePlan.name: Read a night of the Arabian Nights
immersePlan.text: Read one or two nights from Husain Haddawy’s translation of the oldest surviving manuscript, and stop at the cliffhanger. Tell the story to someone later in your own words.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of The House of Wisdom
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Jim Al-Khalili’s story of Arabic science and the translators, told by a physicist born in Baghdad. Pick one scientist and look up another thing about them.

immersePlan.name: Read about a miser in al-Jahiz
immersePlan.text: Open the funniest prose writer of the ninth century and read a few pages of portraits of stingy men. Notice how the humour works, and which one you recognise.

immersePlan.name: Watch an episode of Science and Islam
immersePlan.text: Watch an episode of Jim Al-Khalili’s BBC series on medicine, mathematics or astronomy, filmed in Iraq, Syria and Egypt. Notice what he shows, and what remains.

immersePlan.name: Watch Prince Achmed
immersePlan.text: Watch the oldest surviving animated feature, cut from black paper by hand by Lotte Reiniger in 1926. It is a tale from the Nights. Notice the delicacy of every figure.

immersePlan.name: Watch the Library of Secrets
immersePlan.text: Watch the short film in which a librarian, played by Ben Kingsley, introduces children to the scientists of the Muslim world. It is bright and quick. Notice which inventor you did not know.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Munir Bashir’s oud
immersePlan.text: Play solo improvisations by the Iraqi master who made the oud a concert instrument. Close your eyes and follow the line as it wanders and returns.

immersePlan.name: Hear the Iraqi maqam
immersePlan.text: Play a track of the classical song tradition of Baghdad, with santur, spike fiddle and voice. Notice how a single mode shapes the whole piece.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Rimsky-Korsakov’s Scheherazade
immersePlan.text: Play the Russian composer’s suite inspired by the Nights, with a solo violin as the voice of the storyteller. Pick out the violin every time it comes in.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Malwiya minaret
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the 52-metre baked brick tower with a ramp winding round the outside, built at Samarra around 850. Imagine climbing it.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Maqamat pictures
immersePlan.text: Look at paintings by Yahya al-Wasiti from 1237: lively scenes of libraries, caravans, taverns and villages. Pick one and describe everyone in it.

immersePlan.name: Look at Ibn al-Bawwab’s manuscript
immersePlan.text: Look at the earliest surviving Qur’an on paper in a rounded hand, made in Baghdad in 1000 and 1001. Look at the proportion of the letters, and the evenness of the line.

immersePlan.name: Cook a sikbaj-style stew
immersePlan.text: Stew meat, or chickpeas and vegetables, with vinegar, honey and dried fruit, as in the most praised dish of the court. Taste the sweet and sour together. It is the ancestor of escabeche.

immersePlan.name: Make or taste harisa
immersePlan.text: Make a porridge of wheat and meat beaten smooth and cooked slowly, as sold in the morning markets. A vegetarian version with lentils is fine. Eat it with a spoonful of melted fat or oil.

immersePlan.name: Make almond sweets
immersePlan.text: Make a sweet of almond paste in thin pastry soaked in syrup, scented with rosewater. The sweet that ended a good dinner. Share it with someone.

immersePlan.name: Make a fruit sharab
immersePlan.text: Stir a fruit syrup, pomegranate, quince, rose or lemon, into cold water. The words sherbet, sorbet and syrup come from sharab. Drink it slowly.

immersePlan.name: Make sakanjabin
immersePlan.text: Make a syrup of vinegar and honey with mint and dilute it in water. It is a cooling drink that physicians prescribed, taken diluted in summer. Taste the sour and sweet.

immersePlan.name: Try a malt drink
immersePlan.text: Fuqqa was a lightly fermented barley drink, sold in the streets in sealed jars. Drink a cold non-alcoholic malt drink in its spirit. Taste how it refreshes.

immersePlan.name: Wash hands before and after a meal
immersePlan.text: A servant brought a basin and ewer to each guest in turn at the Abbasid table. Wash your hands slowly before and after one meal today, and offer a basin or a towel to someone else.

immersePlan.name: Play the games of the majlis
immersePlan.text: One guest gives a line of poetry and the next answers with a line. Play a round with a friend, or a round of riddles. Laugh at the stumbles.

immersePlan.name: Lend a book with a note
immersePlan.text: Lend a book to someone who would enjoy it, with a note. Books were lent freely among scholars, and returning one late or damaged was bad form.

immersePlan.name: Play shatranj
immersePlan.text: Play old chess, before the modern queen. The Baghdad courtier al-Suli was the strongest player of his age. Play a short game, with the counsellor moving one step at a time.

immersePlan.name: Play backgammon
immersePlan.text: Play nard, backgammon. Abbasid moralists disapproved of the dice, and everyone played anyway. Play a game with someone and accept the throws.

immersePlan.name: Play a storytelling game
immersePlan.text: Play the storytelling game with a book of numbered paragraphs, or invent one: roll a die, read a short passage, decide what you do. Tell the story afterwards.

immersePlan.name: Spend Friday on al-Mutanabbi Street, in spirit
immersePlan.text: Every Friday the booksellers’ street in Baghdad fills with stalls, readers and poets. Spend time at a bookstall or library near you today, and look for the book that finds you.

immersePlan.name: Mark World Arabic Language Day
immersePlan.text: World Arabic Language Day is on 18 December. Learn to write a word in Arabic, such as the word for book, kitab, and say it aloud.

immersePlan.name: Look up Samarra
immersePlan.text: Look up the caliphs’ capital from 836 to 892: the great mosque and its spiral minaret. Read about a city built and left within fifty years.

immersePlan.name: Think about ilm
immersePlan.text: Ilm is knowledge. Choose one thing you know well enough to teach, and teach it to someone today in five minutes. Notice what you did not know you knew.

immersePlan.name: Hold a small majlis
immersePlan.text: Majlis is a sitting, a salon. Sit with one person and one cup of tea for twenty minutes, with a single question to share. Listen until they finish.

immersePlan.name: Think about zero
immersePlan.text: Sifr is empty, the word from which zero and cipher come. Think about how much depends on the empty place in a number. Find one empty space in your day and protect it.

rules.text: Take the truth from wherever it comes
rules.why: Al-Kindi wrote that nothing should be dearer to the seeker than truth, whatever its source. Today, learn one thing from a person or a people you would not have asked.
Every report in Baghdad travelled with the chain of people who passed it on. When you repeat something today, say where you got it, or say that you do not know.
Ibn al-Haytham made himself the opponent of whatever he read. Test one confident claim today before you pass it on.
Paper made this civilisation possible. A thought not written is lost by the evening. Keep a notebook on you and use it.

rules.text: Argue the point and honour the person
rules.why: The debates had rules: no shouting, no insults, no appeals to your own scripture against someone of another faith. Keep them in every disagreement today.
A host was judged by who was fed. Cook or order for one more than you expect, and find that one.

read.title: The Arabian Nights
read.creator: trans. Husain Haddawy
read.year: stories gathered from the 9th century; this translation 1990
read.why: The core stories from the oldest surviving manuscript, without the later additions. Harun al-Rashid walks the streets of Baghdad in disguise.

read.title: The Book of Misers
read.creator: al-Jahiz, trans. R. B. Serjeant
read.why: Portraits of stingy men from Basra and Khurasan, by the funniest prose writer in Arabic. A window onto ordinary life.

read.title: Mission to the Volga
read.creator: Ibn Fadlan, trans. James E. Montgomery
read.why: A caliph’s envoy travels north from Baghdad and describes the Turks, the Bulghars and a ship burial among the Rus. An eyewitness to the Viking world.

read.title: Impostures
read.creator: al-Hariri, trans. Michael Cooperson
read.why: Fifty tales of a silver-tongued rogue, each rendered in a different kind of English to match the wordplay of the original.

read.title: Stories of Piety and Prayer: Deliverance Follows Adversity
read.creator: al-Tanukhi, trans. Julia Bray
read.why: A judge’s collection of true and half-true stories about people rescued at the last moment.

read.title: The House of Wisdom
read.creator: Jim Al-Khalili
read.why: A physicist born in Baghdad tells the story of Arabic science and the people who made it.

read.title: When Baghdad Ruled the Muslim World
read.creator: Hugh Kennedy
read.why: The court of the caliphs at its height: the palaces, the poets, the harem and the murders.

watch.title: Science and Islam
watch.creator: BBC, presented by Jim Al-Khalili
watch.why: Three episodes on medicine, mathematics and astronomy, filmed in Iraq, Iran, Syria and Egypt.

watch.title: The Adventures of Prince Achmed
watch.creator: Lotte Reiniger
watch.why: The oldest surviving animated feature, cut from black paper by hand and drawn from the Thousand and One Nights.

watch.title: Islam: Empire of Faith
watch.creator: PBS
watch.why: A documentary history from the Prophet to the Ottomans. The second part covers Baghdad and the translation movement.

watch.title: 1001 Inventions and the Library of Secrets
watch.creator: Alan Deakins
watch.why: A thirteen-minute film in which a librarian played by Ben Kingsley introduces schoolchildren to the scientists of the age.

listen.title: The Art of the Oud
listen.creator: Munir Bashir
listen.why: Solo improvisations by the Iraqi master who made the oud a concert instrument.

listen.title: Iraqi maqam
listen.creator: Farida Mohammad Ali and the Iraqi Maqam Ensemble
listen.why: The classical song tradition of Baghdad, with santur, spike fiddle and drum. It is on UNESCO’s list of intangible heritage.

listen.title: In Our Time: The Abbasid Caliphs
listen.creator: BBC Radio 4, with Melvyn Bragg
listen.why: Three historians on the dynasty in forty-five minutes.

listen.title: Scheherazade
listen.creator: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov
listen.why: A Russian composer’s dream of the Nights, with a solo violin as the voice of the storyteller. It shows how Europe imagined Baghdad.

art.title: The spiral minaret of Samarra
art.creator: Great Mosque of Samarra, Iraq
art.why: A tower of baked brick 52 metres high with a ramp winding round the outside. It is called the Malwiya, the twisted one.

art.title: The Maqamat of al-Hariri
art.creator: Painted by Yahya al-Wasiti
art.why: Ninety-nine lively pictures of libraries, caravans, taverns and villages, made in Baghdad two decades before its fall. Bibliothèque nationale de France.

art.title: The Qur’an of Ibn al-Bawwab
art.creator: Baghdad
art.why: The earliest surviving Qur’an on paper in a rounded hand, by the calligrapher who perfected proportioned script. Chester Beatty, Dublin.

art.title: Abbasid lustreware
art.creator: Iraq
art.why: Potters trying to match Chinese porcelain invented a white glaze and a metallic sheen fired onto it. The technique passed to Egypt, Spain and Italy.

art.title: Mustansiriya Madrasa
art.creator: Baghdad, Iraq
art.why: A college for all four Sunni schools of law built beside the Tigris, with a courtyard of pointed arches and brickwork inscriptions.

eat.title: Sikbaj
eat.creator: Meat stewed with vinegar, honey and dried fruit
eat.why: The most praised dish of the court. It travelled west with the Arabs and survives as escabeche.

eat.title: Tharid
eat.creator: Bread soaked in a rich broth
eat.why: Torn flatbread under meat and stock. An old Arabian dish that stayed in favour.

eat.title: Harisa
eat.creator: Wheat and meat beaten to a porridge
eat.why: Cooked overnight and sold in the morning markets, with a spoonful of fat on top.

eat.title: Judhaba
eat.creator: Sweet bread pudding set under roasting chicken
eat.why: A tray of bread, sugar and apricots catches the dripping juices. Sold in the market and loved by poets.

eat.title: Lauzinaj
eat.creator: Almond paste in thin pastry, soaked in syrup
eat.why: The sweet that ended a good dinner, scented with rosewater.

drink.title: Sharab
drink.creator: Fruit syrup stirred into cold water
drink.why: Pomegranate, quince, rose or lemon. The words sherbet, sorbet and syrup all come from it.

drink.title: Sakanjabin
drink.creator: Vinegar and honey syrup with mint
drink.why: A cooling drink that physicians prescribed, taken diluted in summer.

drink.title: Fuqqa
drink.creator: A lightly fermented barley drink
drink.why: Sold in the streets in sealed jars and drunk cold. A malt drink without alcohol stands in.

customs.title: Washing hands at the table
customs.creator: Before and after the meal
customs.why: A servant brought a basin and ewer to each guest in turn. Perfume was offered at the end.

customs.title: Reading for a licence
customs.creator: Studying a book with its teacher
customs.why: You read the whole text aloud to someone who had it from its author’s line, and they wrote their permission on your copy.

customs.title: Riddles and capping verses
customs.creator: Games of the majlis
customs.why: One guest gives a line of poetry and the next must answer with a line that starts on its last letter.

customs.title: Lending a book
customs.creator: With a note of thanks on its return
customs.why: Books were lent freely among scholars, and returning one late or damaged was a known disgrace.

games.title: Shatranj
games.creator: Board game · the Islamic world
games.why: Chess before the modern queen. The Baghdad courtier al-Suli was the strongest player of his century and wrote the first book of opening theory and problems.

games.title: Nard
games.creator: Board game · Persia
games.why: Backgammon. Abbasid moralists disapproved of the dice and everyone played anyway.

games.title: Assassin’s Creed Mirage
games.creator: Video game · Ubisoft Bordeaux
games.why: Set in ninth-century Baghdad, with the round city, the House of Wisdom and the markets rebuilt in detail. A built-in history guide was written with scholars.

games.title: Tales of the Arabian Nights
games.creator: Board game · Eric Goldberg
games.why: A storytelling game with a book of more than two thousand numbered paragraphs. You wander, and things happen to you.

festivals.title: Ramadan nights
festivals.creator: The ninth month of the Islamic calendar
festivals.why: After sunset the city came alive with shared meals, recitation and visiting. The Abbasid caliphs fed crowds at public tables.

festivals.title: Nowruz
festivals.creator: The spring equinox, around 20 March
festivals.why: The Persian new year. The caliphs kept it at court with gifts and bonfires, a sign of how Persian the empire was.

festivals.title: Friday on al-Mutanabbi Street
festivals.creator: Every Friday, Baghdad
festivals.why: The booksellers’ street by the river fills with stalls, readers and poets, as the book market of the city has for a thousand years.

festivals.title: World Arabic Language Day
festivals.creator: 18 December
festivals.why: Marked by UNESCO since 2012 with readings, calligraphy and music.

places.title: Samarra
places.creator: Salah al-Din, Iraq
places.why: The caliphs’ capital from 836 to 892: the great mosque, its spiral minaret and miles of ruined palaces. A World Heritage Site. Check current travel advice for Iraq before planning a visit.

places.title: Mustansiriya Madrasa and al-Mutanabbi Street
places.creator: Baghdad, Iraq
places.why: The thirteenth-century college on the Tigris and, beside it, the street of booksellers. Check current travel advice for Iraq before planning a visit.

places.title: Mosque of Ibn Tulun
places.creator: Cairo, Egypt
places.why: Built from 876 by a governor raised in Samarra, in the Abbasid style, with its own spiral minaret. The best-preserved building of the age.

places.title: Museum of Islamic Art
places.creator: Doha, Qatar
places.why: Abbasid ceramics, glass, astrolabes and manuscripts in a building by I. M. Pei.

places.title: Chester Beatty
places.creator: Dublin, Ireland
places.why: One of the great collections of Arabic manuscripts, including the Qur’an copied by Ibn al-Bawwab in Baghdad.

places.title: House of Wisdom
places.creator: Sharjah, United Arab Emirates
places.why: A public library opened in 2020 and named for its Baghdad ancestor, with exhibitions on the history of the book.

ethics.title: Knowledge is a duty
ethics.text: Seeking knowledge was understood as an obligation on every person and a form of worship. The ink of scholars was praised and learning was pursued across deserts.
ethics.practice: Ask someone today to teach you one thing they know and you do not.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.text: Karam, open-handedness, was the first quality expected of the great. The Barmakid viziers were remembered for centuries for their giving. A full table was a moral achievement.
ethics.practice: Feed someone today who did not expect it.

ethics.title: Good manners in learning
ethics.text: Adab meant knowing how to behave in company: to listen, to speak in turn, to be witty without wounding and to wear learning lightly.
ethics.practice: In your next conversation, ask two questions before you offer an opinion.

ethics.title: Honest weights
ethics.text: Every market had an inspector, the muhtasib, who checked scales, prices and the quality of food. Fair dealing was a public matter.
ethics.practice: Give exact measure today in something small: time owed, change, credit for an idea.

ethics.title: Care for the sick
ethics.text: The hospitals of Baghdad treated anyone, of any faith, without charge, and had separate wards and a pharmacy. Al-Razi wrote a book on medicine for those with no doctor to turn to.
ethics.practice: Visit, call or cook for someone who is unwell.

ethics.title: Humility before the truth
ethics.text: Al-Razi argued that later scholars can surpass the ancients because they add to what was handed down. No one, however great, is beyond correction.
ethics.practice: Tell someone today about a thing you were wrong about.

philosophy.title: Truth has no nation
philosophy.text: Al-Kindi opened his book on first philosophy by thanking the Greeks and arguing that truth should be taken from wherever it is found. The translation movement put this into practice on the scale of an empire.
philosophy.practice: Read one page today from a tradition you know nothing about, looking for what is right in it.

philosophy.title: Reason and revelation
philosophy.text: The Mutazila held that God is just, that people are free and that reason can tell right from wrong. Their opponents answered that reason has limits. The quarrel shaped Islamic theology, and the question is still open in every tradition.
philosophy.practice: Take one belief you hold and write down what reason alone can say for it.

philosophy.title: Doubt as a method
philosophy.text: Ibn al-Haytham held that authorities are human and full of error. The student’s task is to attack what he reads from every side, and also to suspect himself.
philosophy.practice: Argue against your own favourite opinion for five minutes, in writing.

philosophy.title: The experiment
philosophy.text: Asked to choose the site for a hospital, al-Razi is said to have hung meat in different quarters of Baghdad and built where it spoiled last. He also divided patients into groups to compare a treatment.
philosophy.practice: Settle one question today by trying it both ways.

philosophy.title: Translation as creation
philosophy.text: The translators had no Arabic words for many Greek ideas, so they made them. A language was enlarged to hold another civilisation’s thought, and new thought then grew in the room that was made.
philosophy.practice: Explain a term from your own work to someone outside it, without using the term.

philosophy.title: The virtuous city
philosophy.text: Al-Farabi, called the Second Teacher after Aristotle, wrote that people reach their perfection only in a community that is ordered toward knowledge and justice, in which each helps the others toward happiness.
philosophy.practice: Do one thing today that makes the place where you live a little more learned or more just.

philosophy.title: Paper and memory
philosophy.text: Cheap paper meant that a clerk, a cook or a doctor could own books and write them. Knowledge left the palace. The culture of the notebook, the index and the catalogue starts here.
philosophy.practice: Start an index at the back of your notebook.

philosophy.title: The search for certainty
philosophy.text: Al-Ghazali, the most famous professor in Baghdad, found that he could doubt his senses and his reasoning, lost the power to speak and left his post in 1095 to look for what could be known for sure.
philosophy.practice: Write down one thing you are certain of, and how you know it.

intro: In 762 the caliph al-Mansur had a perfectly round city laid out on the west bank of the Tigris and named it the City of Peace. Within two generations Baghdad was probably the largest city in the world outside China, and certainly the most curious. This Onda is about its great age: a culture in love with books, argument, mathematics, medicine, poetry and good food.

The Abbasids took power in 750 from the Umayyads of Damascus, in a revolution that began in eastern Iran. Their empire was Arab in its language and faith and deeply Persian in its style of government. It was served by Muslims, Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians and Sabians. Wealth came down the rivers and across the Indian Ocean. With it came paper, a Chinese invention that reached Baghdad late in the eighth century and made books cheap for the first time anywhere.

What followed has no real precedent. Over about two hundred years, nearly every work of Greek science and philosophy that could be found was translated into Arabic, along with Persian and Indian learning. The work was paid for by caliphs, viziers, doctors and merchants. The translators, many of them Syriac-speaking Christians such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq, built a scientific language as they went. A library and circle of scholars attached to the court became known as the House of Wisdom.

The translations were only the start. Al-Khwarizmi wrote the book that gave algebra its name and introduced Indian numerals to the West. Al-Kindi made philosophy speak Arabic. Al-Razi ran the hospital in Baghdad and wrote case notes that told smallpox apart from measles. Astronomers measured the Earth. Ibn al-Haytham, born in Basra, worked out how vision works by experiment. Around them were grammarians, historians, cooks who wrote recipe books, and al-Jahiz, who wrote about everything.

It was not a paradise. The court was violent, and one caliph ran an inquisition over a point of theology. The empire’s southern estates were worked by enslaved East Africans, whose revolt from 869 lasted fourteen years. From the tenth century the caliphs lost real power to their own soldiers and then to outside dynasties. In February 1258 a Mongol army took Baghdad, killed the last caliph and wrecked the city. Much of what it had learned had already travelled, to Cairo, Córdoba, Samarkand and, in Latin, to the universities of Europe.

The practices here follow the habits of its scholars and hosts. You will study each morning, translate a paragraph, test one claim a day, hold a gathering in the evening and look at the stars. This Onda is about a civilisation and its love of knowledge. It is not instruction in Islam, which is a living faith with its own teachers.
guide.origin: Baghdad on the Tigris, capital of an empire that reached from North Africa to Central Asia
guide.era: The Abbasid caliphate, 750 to 1258, at its height in the ninth and tenth centuries

figures.name: al-Mansur
figures.bio: The second Abbasid caliph and founder of Baghdad. Thrifty, hard and far-sighted, he collected books and had astrologers choose the day building began.

figures.name: Harun al-Rashid
figures.bio: Caliph at the empire’s richest moment and the ruler of the Thousand and One Nights. He exchanged embassies with Charlemagne and sent him an elephant.

figures.name: al-Mamun
figures.bio: The scholar-caliph. He funded translation and observatories, had the Earth measured, and also forced a theological test on judges and scholars.

figures.name: Zubayda
figures.bio: Wife of Harun al-Rashid. She paid for wells, cisterns and rest houses along the pilgrim road from Kufa to Mecca, which is still called by her name.

figures.name: al-Khwarizmi
figures.bio: Mathematician and astronomer. His book on completion and balancing founded algebra, and his own name, in Latin, became the word algorithm.

figures.name: Hunayn ibn Ishaq
figures.bio: A Christian physician from al-Hira and the greatest of the translators. He put more than a hundred works of Galen into Syriac and Arabic and was said to be paid their weight in gold.

figures.name: al-Kindi
figures.bio: The philosopher of the Arabs. He wrote on everything from metaphysics to music and perfume, and described how to break a cipher by counting letters.

figures.name: al-Jahiz
figures.bio: A prose writer from Basra, grandson of an East African. His books on animals, misers and eloquence are sharp, digressive and funny.

figures.name: The Banu Musa
figures.bio: Three brothers, sons of a reformed highwayman, who measured the Earth for al-Mamun, hired translators and wrote a book of ingenious mechanical devices.

figures.name: Arib al-Mamuniyya
figures.bio: The most famous singer, poet and composer of the court. She served under several caliphs and was credited with a thousand songs.

figures.name: al-Razi
figures.bio: Physician and hospital director, known in Latin as Rhazes. He kept clinical notes, doubted Galen where the evidence required and wrote for the poor.

figures.name: Ibn al-Nadim
figures.bio: A Baghdad bookseller who catalogued every book he had seen or heard of in Arabic. Thousands of lost works are known only from his list.

figures.name: Ibn al-Haytham
figures.bio: Born in Basra and active in Cairo. His Book of Optics showed by experiment that we see because light enters the eye.

figures.name: al-Ghazali
figures.bio: Jurist, theologian and mystic. He left a famous chair in Baghdad in a crisis of doubt and wrote the most influential religious books of medieval Islam.

history.detail: An army from Khurasan under black banners defeated the Umayyad caliph on the river Zab. A new dynasty, descended from the Prophet’s uncle, took the caliphate and moved its centre east to Iraq.
Tradition holds that Chinese papermakers captured at the battle of Talas brought their craft to Samarkand. Whatever the route, paper mills were working in Baghdad before the century was out.
Al-Mansur laid out a round city about two kilometres across, with four gates and his palace and mosque at the centre. The first brick was laid on 30 July, a day chosen by his astrologers.
The empire at its richest. The Barmakid family of viziers ran the state and paid for scholars and poets, until Harun destroyed them in 803.
After a civil war against his brother, al-Mamun made the court a centre of science. Greek works were sought as far away as Constantinople, and observatories were built in Baghdad and Damascus.
Al-Khwarizmi wrote his short book on calculation by completion and balancing for the caliph, with worked problems on inheritance, trade and surveying.
Al-Mamun and his successors required judges and scholars to affirm that the Qur’an was created. The jurist Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused and was flogged. The policy failed and was dropped.
The caliphs moved their court and their Turkish soldiers to a new city up the Tigris and built on a vast scale before returning to Baghdad.
Enslaved East Africans who had been forced to clear the salt marshes of southern Iraq rose under a leader named Ali ibn Muhammad. They sacked Basra and held out for fourteen years.
An Iranian dynasty took control of the capital. The caliph kept his title and little else. Learning went on flourishing under new patrons.
The Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded a college in Baghdad with salaried professors and funded students. It became the model for the madrasa.
The Nizamiyya’s most celebrated teacher found himself unable to lecture, gave away his wealth and left the city. He was away for a decade.
One of the last caliphs founded a college on the Tigris with a library, a hospital and a water clock. Its building still stands.
The Mongol army of Hulegu took the city in February after a short siege, killed the caliph al-Mustasim and a great many of the inhabitants, and destroyed libraries. The caliphate in Iraq ended.

concepts.text: The caliphs’ library and its circle.
concepts.detail: Later writers pictured a great academy. The early evidence points to a palace library where translators, astronomers and copyists worked under royal pay. Whatever its size, the name stands for a real thing: state support for knowledge on a scale the world had not seen.

concepts.text: Greek, Persian and Indian learning into Arabic.
concepts.detail: It lasted from the mid-eighth to the late tenth century and was paid for across the whole of elite society. Translators compared manuscripts, revised earlier versions and invented a technical vocabulary. Aristotle, Galen, Euclid and Ptolemy survive in part because of it.

Rag paper cost a fraction of parchment and could not be scraped clean and altered, which made it ideal for records. It created professional copyists, bookshops, private libraries and the habit of writing things down.

concepts.text: The culture of the well-bred mind.
concepts.detail: A body of literature and a way of behaving. The educated person knew poetry, history, proverbs and a little of every science, and could use them with grace. Many of the best Abbasid books are anthologies made to teach it.

concepts.text: The party of justice and unity.
concepts.detail: Theologians who argued that God must be just, that people are therefore responsible for what they do and that scripture should be read in the light of reason. Favoured and then abandoned by the court, they left their methods to all later theology.
Founded by caliphs and viziers and paid for by endowments, with wards for different illnesses, a pharmacy, bedside teaching and written records. Patients were treated free, whatever their religion.
Scholars of prophetic tradition tested each report by its chain of transmitters and the character of each link. The habit of citing sources spread from them into history, law and literature.
Al-Khwarizmi solved equations in words, without symbols, by two moves: restoring a subtracted quantity to the other side and balancing like terms. He proved each rule with a geometric figure.

Al-Mansur’s city was a circle with the ruler at the centre and roads to the four quarters of the empire. Nothing of it remains above ground. Within decades the life of the city had spilled far outside its walls.

A gathering under a host for debate, poetry or music. Its etiquette allowed people of different schools and faiths to argue in public. Records of these sessions are among the liveliest writing of the age.

facts.text: The word algorithm is al-Khwarizmi’s name as it was spelled in medieval Latin. Algebra comes from the title of his book.
Harun al-Rashid sent Charlemagne an elephant named Abul-Abbas, which reached the emperor’s court at Aachen in 802.
Aldebaran, Altair, Vega, Deneb, Rigel and Betelgeuse are all Arabic names. So are the words zenith, nadir and azimuth.
Al-Mamun’s astronomers measured one degree of latitude on a plain in northern Iraq and arrived at a figure for the Earth’s circumference that was close to the true one.
Al-Jahiz is said to have died in his nineties when a stack of books fell on him.
Baghdad’s tenth-century cookbook, by Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq, contains more than six hundred recipes, with poems in praise of the dishes.
Coffee was unknown in Abbasid Baghdad. It arrived from Yemen several centuries later.

sensitivity.note: Abbasid Baghdad was the work of Arabs, Persians, Syriac Christians, Jews and many others, within a Muslim empire. Its learning is part of the heritage of people living today, in Iraq above all. This Onda explores the culture of knowledge of that time. It is not instruction in Islam, and it does not treat the period as a lost golden age.
requiredCaveats: The empire rested in part on conquest and on slavery. The Zanj revolt and the violence of the court are part of the story.
Golden age is a later label. Learning in Arabic did not stop in 1258, and it flourished in many cities besides Baghdad.
Islam is a living faith. Its beliefs and practices are for its own teachers to explain; nothing here imitates worship.
Much of what is said about the House of Wisdom comes from later writers, and historians disagree about how much to believe.
This content has not yet been reviewed by historians of the period or by people from Iraq. It should be before release.
